source.title: What training reveals about neural network complexity
source.authors: Andreas Loukas; Marinos Poiitis; S. Jegelka

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures links between training dynamics, Lipschitz complexity, and held-out test loss using different tasks and measures from the claim versions; its own empirical results bear on V7 and on architecture and batch-size conditions related to V3 and V5.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own empirical comparisons of bias-trajectory measures with test loss, and its explicit statement about which architecture overfits less. Theorems and cited findings are not empirical rows. Values available only in plots are recorded as figure only; the supplied text gives no exact numeric values for them.
record.test_reason: The MNIST experiment directly compares CNN and MLP generalization under SGD, bearing on V3 through held-out loss and overfitting. Bias trajectories and bias variance do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness; the regression batch-size experiment does not test V5's fixed-epoch classification or language-model claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors theoretically connect small local Lipschitz constants with shorter normalized first-layer bias trajectories and lower bias variation, provide supporting experiments, and suggest that steady training may indicate good generalization. Their dropout generalization bound is conditional on stated assumptions; they do not establish the magnitude-aware sharpness claim.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies normalized first-layer bias trajectories and local Lipschitz complexity, using synthetic sinusoidal regression, CIFAR10 label corruption, and an MNIST architecture comparison; it does not run the original interventions or measurements in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Task complexity/frequency and label-corruption rate change the trajectory and test-loss relationship; architecture and training-set size are varied in MNIST; batch sizes 1, 16 and 32 affect the reported trajectory measure.

fits_no_version.finding: Longer normalized first-layer bias trajectories accompany more complex fitted functions and poorer held-out performance across the tested synthetic-frequency and label-corruption conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalized first-layer bias-trajectory length can indicate learned-function complexity and held-out loss in these tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: The small-data MNIST MLP has a longer bias trajectory than the CNN; trajectory and loss are also plotted for the larger training set.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bias trajectories can serve as a diagnostic of differences in learned-function complexity between architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic regression, increasing batch size from 1 to 32 slightly increases trajectory length, and trajectory length remains associated with task complexity and test loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The bias-trajectory diagnostic varies with batch size in the tested regression setup.

fits_no_version.finding: First-layer bias variance near convergence increases with task complexity in synthetic regression and corrupted-label CIFAR classification.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bias variation during late SGD training reflects learned-function complexity in these tasks.

record.problems: Empirical comparisons are limited to two tasks and a small set of architectures. Most plotted outcomes have no exact values or uncertainty estimates in the supplied text. The architecture result is a single small-data MNIST comparison. The paper explicitly says it lacks mathematical evidence for the observed batch-size increase in trajectory length. Its empirical trajectory measures do not test magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows were omitted. Rows R4 and R6 preserve figure-only comparisons where the text gives no directional conclusion.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy under matched architectures and recipes.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error and the resulting test-error behavior.

Local connectivity as the cause of the advantage; learned sparse local connections; initialization from trained convolutional networks; comparisons on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and SVHN. The supplied text does not resolve the MNIST1000 comparison.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizers and the effects of tuning, weight decay or optimizer switching.
Held-out performance penalties from large batches under fixed epoch budgets on image or language workloads, and recipe changes that remove them.
Comparative held-out error with and without dropout. The conditional generalization bound for dropout is not an empirical dropout-benefit comparison.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its correlation with training–test gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and measuring retrained test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V3. MNIST is already within V3's stated datasets. Missing measurements of sharpness or fixed-epoch batch penalties warrant untested entries, not limits_scope verdicts. Plot coordinates cannot be reconstructed reliably from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization versus natural-label test accuracy.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test-error behavior.
The MNIST experiment compares one MLP and one CNN, not the listed datasets or local-connectivity interventions.
Only bias-trajectory behavior at batch sizes 16 and 32 is compared; no stated comparison of test performance at fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.stage_stated: trained with SGD until it had fit the sinusoidal function
rows.operation_detail: Compared normalized first-layer bias trajectory length with held-out test loss across sinusoidal frequencies.

conditions.value: regression of randomly sampled 2D sinusoidal function isometrically embedded in 10 dimensions

rows.measure: Held-out test loss, related to normalized bias-trajectory length
rows.value: Longer trajectories consistently corresponded to poorer test performance; figure values only.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the trajectory and test-loss correlation; exact values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: Normalized bias-trajectory length is not magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, and test loss is not the training–test gap. The reported correlation cannot establish V7. The original experiment used batch size 1, as Appendix A.6 states.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.operation_detail: Compared normalized first-layer bias trajectory length with held-out test loss across label-corruption rates.

conditions.value: binary CIFAR10 classification, dog and airplane classes

rows.measure: Held-out test loss, related to normalized bias-trajectory length
rows.value: Longer trajectories consistently corresponded to poorer test performance; figure values only.
rows.note: Text describes the correlation across corruption settings; no exact test-loss values are stated.
rows.check: Neither magnitude-aware sharpness nor its ranking of generalization gaps is measured. Partial label corruption also does not establish V1's natural-label versus fixed-random-label comparison.

measures computed over intervals of 100 iterations

rows.measure: Training loss, normalized bias-trajectory length, and test loss
rows.baseline: The MLP is the architecture comparator for the CNN.
rows.value: With the small training set, both architectures fit the training data equally well after roughly 20k iterations, but the CNN overfits less; the MLP has a longer trajectory. Figure values only.
rows.locator: Appendix A.5, Figure 8a–c and accompanying text
rows.note: The text says the CNN overfits less and the MLP learns a more complex function as indicated by the longer trajectory; exact values appear only in plots.
rows.check: The stated equal training fit and lower CNN overfitting support the architectural comparison. Narrow dataset coverage does not make the observed effect partial. This comparison duplicates R9; consolidate their generalization evidence while retaining trajectory measurements separately.

rows.value: Both fit the training data equally well after roughly 20k iterations, but the CNN overfits less.

relationships.condition: Binary MNIST classification of digits 3 and 6, with 100 training images per class and SGD
relationships.reason: R9 reports that the CNN overfits less than the MLP after both fit the training data equally well at roughly 20,000 iterations; R3 records the same comparison.
relationships.display_finding: The reported lower CNN overfitting after comparable training fit remains unverified.
